header.title: Argonautica: AI translation (Claude)
header.author: Apollonius Rhodius
header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's tlg0001.tlg001.perseus-grc2, from the Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. Only some passages are translated so far: those that the Atlas of Ancient Myth, Magic in the Ancient Texts and the demons-and-angels study cite.

notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg0001.tlg001.perseus-: νήχυτον ὕδωρ (530) is rendered 'flowing water'; the sense of the adjective ('flowing' or 'abundant') is uncertain.
ἐμέγηρεν (1670), literally 'grudged', is taken as casting the evil eye; ἀίδηλα (1671) may mean 'destructive' or 'unseen'.
ἀδαίετον (1033) may mean 'undivided' or 'unburnt'; 'whole' is chosen.
ὑποφήτορες (22) is rendered 'interpreters'; whether the Muses here prompt the poet or speak through him is disputed.
κευθμῶν ἐξ ὑπάτων (1213): ὕπατος usually means 'highest'; here it is taken as 'utmost', of the deepest recesses.
ἀτρέπτοιο φόνοιο (704), literally 'unturnable murder', is rendered 'inexorable'; it may mean a killing not yet expiated. τιμήορον (709) can mean 'avenger' or 'protector'.

nodes.text: Beginning with you, Phoebus, the glorious deeds of men born long ago
I shall recall, who through the mouth of the Pontus and between
the Cyanean Rocks, at the command of King Pelias,
of the heroes, and the paths of the long sea, and all that they did
in their wanderings; and may the Muses be the interpreters of my song.
First, then, let us call to mind Orpheus, whom once she herself,
Calliope, it is said, having lain with Thracian
Oeagrus, bore near the Pimpleian height.
and they meanwhile ruled over the blessed gods, the Titans,
while Zeus was still a boy, still with childish thoughts in his mind,
and dwelt in the Dictaean cave; and not yet had they,
the earth-born Cyclopes, armed him with the thunderbolt,
with thunder and lightning; for these give Zeus his glory.
began a clear song to his Bistonian lyre:
how once beneath the rocky ridge of Parnassus
he slew with his arrows the monstrous Delphyne,
while still a naked boy, still delighting in his locks.
Be gracious! Always, lord, your hair is unshorn,
easy: such a serpent guards it round about,
deathless and sleepless, which Earth herself brought forth
on the slopes of the Caucasus, where Typhon's Rock is,
where they say that Typhon, by the thunderbolt of Zeus, son of Cronus,
struck, when he raised his mighty hands against him,
dripped hot blood from his head; and in that state he reached
the mountains and the plain of Nysa, where even now
he lies submerged beneath the waters of the Serbonian lake.
So he spoke; and pallor seized the cheeks of many
at once, when they heard of such a contest. But quickly Peleus
is better than to choose an evil doom by not sparing ourselves.
There is a girl brought up in the halls of Aeetes,
whom the goddess Hecate taught surpassingly to work with
drugs, all that the mainland and the flowing water grow;
by them even the blast of tireless fire is soothed,
and she stops rivers at once as they flow roaring,
and binds fast the stars and the paths of the holy moon.
Of her, as we came here along the path from the palace,
we made mention, in case she, being her sister, might be able
the flesh-devouring eagle, on the slopes of the Caucasus,
the bloody ichor of tormented Prometheus.
Its flower, about a cubit high above [the ground],
appeared in colour like the Corycian crocus,
raised on twin stalks; but in the earth
the root was like flesh newly cut.
Its juice, dark like the sap of an oak in the mountains,
she had gathered in a Caspian shell to make her drug,
after bathing seven times in ever-flowing waters
and seven times calling on Brimo, nurse of the young,
Brimo the night-wanderer, of the underworld, queen among the dead,
in the gloom of night, in dark garments.
And with a bellowing the black earth shook beneath
as the Titanian root was cut; and he himself groaned,
the son of Iapetus, his spirit distraught with pain.
This she had taken out and placed in the fragrant band
which was fastened round her ambrosial breast.
When my father, on your coming to him, puts into your hands
the deadly teeth from the serpent's jaws to sow,
then, watching for the middle of the night, when it is divided in two,
having bathed in the streams of the tireless river,
alone, apart from others, in dark garments,
dig a rounded pit; and in it a female
sheep slaughter, and lay it out whole as a raw offering,
having piled a pyre well over the pit itself.
And propitiate Hecate, the only-begotten daughter of Perses,
pouring from a cup the hive-stored work of bees.
Then, when you have called the goddess to mind and propitiated her,
withdraw back from the pyre; and let neither the thud
of feet rouse you to turn around behind you,
nor the baying of dogs, lest somehow, spoiling everything,
you yourself do not return in proper order to your comrades.
At dawn, moisten this drug, and like an ointment,
stripped bare, rub it over your body; and in it there will be prowess
boundless, and great strength, and you would say you were a match not
for men but for the immortal gods.
And besides, let your shield be sprinkled, along with the spear itself,
and your sword. Then the points would not cut you
putting fire beneath, and over it he poured mingled libations,
calling on Brimo Hecate as helper in his contests.
And having called on her he went back; and she, hearing,
the dread goddess, came from the utmost depths to meet
the rites of the son of Aeson; and all around her were wreathed
terrible serpents among oak boughs.
And the boundless blaze of torches flashed; and around her
the hounds of the underworld howled with shrill barking.
All the meadows trembled along her path; and they cried aloud,
the marsh-dwelling river nymphs, who around that
her among the guards, and she escaped their notice as she sped.
From there she resolved to go to the temple; for she was not unacquainted
with the roads, having often roamed before around corpses
and around the stubborn roots of the earth, as women
who are sorceresses do; and her heart quivered with trembling fear.
And as the Titanian one, newly rising from the far horizon,
saw her wandering in frenzy, the goddess Mene [the Moon] gloated over her
with glee, and spoke such words in her own heart:
'So I am not the only one to slip away to the Latmian cave,
nor do I alone burn for handsome Endymion;
truly, often have I gone away at your guileful incantations,
thinking of my love, so that in the dark night
you might work your sorcery at ease, the deeds that are dear to you.
But now you yourself, it seems, have your share of a like madness;
and has given you Jason to be a grievous affliction,
the chieftains, on the advice of Argus, set ashore.
And the two came by a footpath to the sacred grove,
seeking the vast oak on which the fleece
was hung, like a cloud that at the rising
sun's fiery rays turns red.
But right opposite, he stretched out his huge long neck,
raising its terrible head on high, it was eager
to enfold both of them in its deadly jaws.
But she, with a newly cut sprig of juniper
dipping pure drugs from the brew, with incantations
sprinkled them over its eyes; and all around, the immense scent
of the drug cast sleep; and its jaw, in that very place,
it laid down, resting it; and far behind, those endless
coils were stretched out through the thick-trunked wood.

And the two of them were agreeing with each other on every point;
and at once the son of Aeson sprang out of the close ambush,
raising his naked sword in his hand; and at once the girl
turned her eyes away, veiling herself in linen,
so as not to see the slaughter of her brother as he was struck.
And him, as an ox-slaughterer [strikes] a great strong-horned bull,
he struck, having watched for him, near the temple which once
the Brygi who dwell around, on the mainland opposite, built for Artemis.
she performed the sacrifice by which are cleansed
ruthless suppliants when they come to the hearth.
First, as a release from the inexorable murder, she
stretched out above [them] the young of a sow whose teats still
were brimming from the womb newly delivered, and their hands with blood
she wetted, cutting its throat; and again with other
libations she made propitiation, invoking as Purifier
Zeus, the protector of the supplications of the blood-guilty.
And all the defilements together they carried out of the house,
the Naiad attendants, who saw to every task for her.

A steady wind carried the ship. And soon an island,
a fair one, Anthemoessa, they beheld, where the clear-voiced
Sirens, daughters of Achelous, would destroy, with their sweet
songs enchanting him, whoever cast a mooring-rope there.
they kept searching for a spring; for a parching
thirst lay on them, besides their hardship and pains; and not in vain
did they wander. They came to the holy plain where Ladon,
until only yesterday, it seems, guarded the all-golden apples
in the land of Atlas, the serpent of the earth; and around him the nymphs,
the Hesperides, busied themselves, singing their lovely song.
But by then, at that very time, struck down by Heracles,
he lay flung against the trunk of the apple tree; only with the tip
of his tail was he still writhing; but from his head along his dark
Carpathus; and from there they meant to cross over
to Crete, which surpasses the other islands in the sea.
But bronze Talos, from the massive crag
breaking off rocks, kept them from tying their cables to the land
as they came into the sheltering anchorage of Dicte.
Him, of the bronze race of men sprung from ash trees
the one left over from that stock among the men who were demigods,
the son of Cronus gave to Europa to be the warden of the island,
striding three times around Crete on his bronze feet.
Now, the rest of his body and his limbs were made
she went up onto the deck; and grasping her hand in his hand,
the son of Aeson guided her as she went between the benches.
There with songs she sought to appease, and hymned the *Kēres* [spirits of death],
heart-devouring, swift hounds of Hades, who, through all
the air whirling, are driven against the living.
Beseeching them, three times she called on them with songs,
three times with prayers; and, setting her mind to evil, with hostile
eyes she cast the evil eye on the eyes of bronze Talos;
against him she ground out baleful wrath, and sent forth
destructive phantoms, in vehement fury.
Father Zeus, truly great wonder stirs in my mind,
if indeed destruction [comes upon us] not only by diseases and wounds
